previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with chronic lymphedema, morbid obesity, and a history of recurrent cellulitis was admitted for worsening bilateral leg swelling extending into the thighs and lower back, despite recent treatment with ceftriaxone and outpatient diuretics. Imaging ruled out deep vein thrombosis, and CT of the thigh revealed varicose veins without a mass. She was treated with IV furosemide, leading to improved edema. During the hospitalization, she developed a cough and rising white blood cell count; a repeat chest X-ray showed left lower lobe pneumonia, prompting a course of levofloxacin. She also experienced an anaphylactic reaction to Lumason during an echocardiogram, which was treated promptly and added to her allergy list. Her home diuretic, bumetanide, was resumed, and she was discharged on oral antibiotics, penicillin prophylaxis, and all prior medications. She was referred to allergy and lymphedema clinics for follow-up.

Dear Ms. ___,

What was done for me while I was in the hospital?
You were admitted because you had increased redness and swelling 
in your legs.

What was done for me while I was in the hospital?

We also had our lymphedema team evaluate you in order to wrap 
you legs tightly. We treated you with a course of antibiotics. 
Ultimately our physical therapists evaluated you and felt you 
would do best if you went to a rehab facility for a short time 
prior to removing home.

What should I do when I leave the hospital?
You should continue taking all of your medications as 
prescribed. If you notice fevers or worsening pain in your legs 
please call your PCP. As we discussed, we will leave your pain 
regimen as it currently stands.

We wish you the best in your recovery!
Your ___ treatment team
